items.title: Dating App Contact Becomes Third Alleged Victim in Mississauga Trafficking Case, Police Say
items.summary: According to CTV News, Toronto police have laid additional charges against a Mississauga man accused of human trafficking after two more alleged victims came forward. Police say Elijah Benjamin was first taken into custody on July 22 and was re-arrested on July 30 after investigators identified further allegations, and he now faces charges including procuring, trafficking in persons by recruiting, advertising another person's sexual services, living on the avails of prostitution, material benefit from sexual services, assault with a weapon and two counts of assault. CTV News reports investigators allege Benjamin coerced one victim into taking sexually explicit photos that were then distributed online, and that she was made to surrender the money she earned to him. Police allege he did the same thing to a second victim, a 32-year-old woman. CTV News reports that earlier this month, investigators learned Benjamin had also tried to recruit a 31-year-old woman he met through an online dating app into the sex trade.

items.title: New AGM Exhibition Turns One Artist's Family Archives Into a Story of Displacement
items.summary: According to Mississauga.com, the Art Gallery of Mississauga is opening a new exhibition this Saturday that draws directly on one artist's family archives to explore displacement and memory. The show, titled Electric Neon Clock, comes from artist Kobayashi, who used personal family records to examine the forced incarceration and dispossession of Japanese Canadians during the Second World War. Mississauga.com reports the exhibition was curated by the gallery's senior curator, Shannon Anderson, and pairs visual art with a live performance component. Opening day includes a community launch and reception alongside an origami boat workshop, held in partnership with Japan Festival Canada. Gallery organizers describe the show as an immersive experience intended to give visitors a closer look at Japanese Canadian history and culture. Mississauga.com notes the exhibit gives Mississauga residents a chance to engage with a chapter of Canadian history that isn't always widely taught, told through documents drawn from one family's own past.

items.title: Lithium-Ion Batteries Are Now Mississauga's Fastest-Growing Fire Risk, Fire Crews Say
items.summary: According to the City of Mississauga, Mississauga Fire and Emergency Services has identified lithium-ion batteries as the city's fastest-growing ignition source, recording a 122 per cent jump in battery-related fires in 2025 compared to the year before. The city says MFES responded to 20 lithium-ion battery incidents in 2025 and has already responded to 15 so far this year. Officials note these batteries power everyday devices like cell phones, laptops, e-bikes and power tools, and are generally safe when used properly, but damaged, defective or improperly charged batteries can pose a serious fire risk. The City of Mississauga explains that damaged batteries can sometimes undergo thermal runaway, a chain reaction that produces intense heat, fire, toxic gases and, in some cases, explosions. MFES is urging residents to follow safe charging, storage and disposal practices, and to stop using a battery or device immediately if they notice warning signs such as swelling, unusual odours, excessive heat, discolouration, leaking fluid, smoke, vapour or strange noises. The city adds that anyone whose battery catches fire should move away from it and call 911.

items.title: Ford's Backing of Parrish for Mississauga Mayor May Be Working Against Her, New Poll Suggests
items.summary: According to the Toronto Star, a new Liaison Strategies poll suggests Mississauga Mayor Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie are locked in a dead heat heading into the fall election, even though Ontario Premier Doug Ford has publicly backed Parrish's campaign. The poll, released Friday, found Parrish and Crombie would each take 26 per cent of the vote if the Oct. 26 election were held today, with another 26 per cent of voters still undecided. Councillors Dipika Damerla and Alvin Tedjo trailed with 13 per cent and nine per cent respectively, according to the poll. The Star reports Liaison principal David Valentin said none of the candidates has made a clear case for why voters should choose them over the others, leaving a large pool of undecided voters still up for grabs amid a broader sense the city is heading in the wrong direction. The Star notes an October 2025 Liaison poll also found Crombie and Parrish tied in a then-hypothetical matchup, before Crombie left to lead the Ontario Liberals and later resigned after the party's provincial election loss. Candidate registration for the fall municipal elections opened Friday as well.

items.title: Grounded for Four Years, Russian Cargo Jet at Pearson Loses Latest Court Bid to Fly Free
items.summary: According to INsauga, a Federal Court judge has rejected the latest legal challenge from the Russian company that owns a massive cargo plane stranded at Toronto Pearson Airport in Mississauga for more than four years. The aircraft, an Antonov An-124 and one of the largest cargo planes in the world, has sat grounded at Pearson since February 2022, when Canada closed its airspace to Russian-owned aircraft shortly after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. INsauga reports the federal government went a step further in June 2023, formally seizing the plane as part of its sanctions against Russia, with Ottawa saying it eventually wants to transfer the aircraft to Ukraine. The plane's registered owner, Volga-Dnepr Airlines, described as Russia's largest air cargo carrier, asked the Federal Court to review Ottawa's decision to keep sanctions in place against the company and its former chairman. INsauga notes the airline had argued in a 2023 application that it should be removed from Canada's sanctions list because it stopped carrying military cargo back in 2018. The federal government rejected that argument, countering that Volga-Dnepr had continued benefiting from Russian government contracts and subsidies and had helped President Vladimir Putin's regime get around sanctions. With the judge's ruling, the legal fight over the plane's fate continues, and the Antonov remains parked at Pearson for now.
